author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Where the Water Cannot Go
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
Fen spread three maps on the table and weighted them down with stones.

The oldest showed a blue line running beneath the square toward Tideglass. The second, drawn after the Closed Bells, ended that line in thick black ink. The third was ours, covered in flood marks, inspection dates, and the small angry circles Tamsin drew wherever a repair still needed money.

"Water doesn't disappear because somebody closes a door," Fen said.

Toph tapped the table.

"Neither do the consequences."

I stood beside Maui, watching Fen trace the old route.

Before the sealing, the passage had carried excess rainwater away from the terraces and floodplain into a controlled coastal outlet during certain tide conditions. It wasn't a miracle. It had gates, inspections, and periods when it couldn't be used safely. After the lower barrier was sealed, the valley had relied on smaller surface drains and a series of improvised diversions.

The diversions worked in ordinary weather.

In storms, they pushed water toward the same homes and gardens again and again.

Sela pointed to the map.

"Mine."

Then another point.

"Mine too. I thought the floods were just getting worse."

"They may be," Fen said. "But the blocked route has made the pattern less forgiving."

Neri sat at the far end of the table with a stack of copied maintenance receipts. Their face was pale.

"The council kept repairing the surface channels," they said. "We told ourselves we were improving the valley."

"You were repairing symptoms," Tamsin answered. "Sometimes repairs were necessary. They weren't the whole plan."

I felt a cold ache beneath my ribs.

The old decision had not ended when the keepers died or the records burned. It had become a pattern in the landscape, the kind people accepted because they had lived with it long enough.

Maui stared at the map.

"Then open the barrier."

Fen shook their head.

"Not yet."

"People are getting wet."

"And they'd get much wetter if an unstable tunnel failed under the spring."

The silence was uncomfortable.

Danse laid out the inspection results from the upper chamber. The mortar was different in two sections. One support showed long-term movement. We could test the surface outlet and keep the temporary channels open, but the lower route required engineering work before any attempt at full reopening.

I wanted to argue.

Instead I asked what the current closure actually meant.

"The upper maintenance hatch can be opened under supervision for inspection," Tamsin said. "The lower flood barrier remains closed. Surface drains need additional capacity before the next storm."

Edda raised her hand.

"And the detour must be usable by people who can't take the steps to the upper ridge."

We rewrote the work list.

The council would fund an accessible temporary path and a monitored surface overflow. Tideglass would provide tide data, Riverstone would oversee drainage effects on gardens, Brasswatch would test the portable pump and new fittings, and Moonroot would preserve the old plans without claiming they gave anyone permission to enter unsafe spaces.

The work needed money and patience.

Neither was popular.

After the meeting, I found Neri by the fountain.

They were staring at the old stone arch.

"I used to think the sealed route was part of our history," they said. "Something unfortunate and finished."

"It wasn't finished."

"No."

They looked at me.

"Do you hate me for not asking sooner?"

I had to think before answering.

"I'm angry that people kept suffering. I'm glad you're asking now. Both are true."

They nodded slowly.

"That is more than I expected."

The temporary channel was built over the following week. It ran along the safe upper path, using removable sections that could be cleaned without entering the old tunnel. Sela helped place the runoff markers near the garden. Edda tested the detour in wet weather. Toph checked the supports while Tamsin logged the movement.

Maui carried materials when asked and learned the names of three workers who had previously been invisible to him. He brought hot food from the pantry after the late shift, then stayed to wash the pots.

The work did not make him smaller.

I was beginning to think it made him more himself.

On the final test day, a controlled flow of water ran through the temporary channel and out toward the coast. Fen watched the gauges. Danse checked the pump. Sela stood beside the garden, waiting to see whether her soil would flood again.

The first test passed.

The second revealed a small leak near the lower joint.

We stopped and repaired it.

The third passed within the limits the team had written down.

Nobody cheered until Fen said the words.

"Safe for the posted conditions."

Then we cheered.

The cheering stopped as soon as Fen asked us to record the test conditions.

"If the tide rises past the marked line, close the channel. If the debris screen blocks, close it until it's cleared. If nobody on duty answers, don't improvise."

Maui rested on his shovel. "You have an extraordinary talent for ruining celebrations."

"And keeping people alive for the next one," Fen answered.

Sela asked about frozen winter ground. Fen admitted the team had no winter data. Rather than declare permanent success, they wrote down what needed monitoring. Edda tested the route in the evening light and pointed out a marker that disappeared against the wet paving. Tamsin moved it, then asked her to try again.

Neri posted three notices: the approved operating conditions, the name of each duty worker, and a private route for residents to report flooding. Nobody would have to post a home address or a medical need beside the bakery menu. Two people outside the repair crew would review disputes.

"That seems rather formal," Maui said.

"Water can be extremely formal when it reaches somebody's kitchen," Sela replied.

Even Danse smiled.

A child asked whether the new channel would stay forever. Fen crouched beside the diagram.

"We don't know. We test things, fix them, and sometimes replace them."

"So something can work without being finished?"

"Especially that," Toph said.

We put the tools away before rain arrived. The unknown signature in Moonroot's Closed Bells records was still unknown, and no newly approved surface test gave us permission to cross the old underground barrier. But for tonight Sela could go home with a dry garden and Edda could use the path. That felt worth celebrating properly.


The lower passage remained closed.

That evening, Maui found me sitting on the bench above Tideglass. I was tired enough that the sea seemed to move in slow pieces.

"Disappointed?" he asked.

"A little."

"Because we didn't open the old route?"

"Yes."

He sat beside me.

"Me too."

I leaned against him.

"But the gardens are safer," I said.

"And people can use the path."

"And the inspection records are public."

He smiled.

"Not exactly a great legend."

"Perhaps we should stop measuring our lives by whether they make good legends."

He pretended to consider.

"That sounds like more work."

"It is."

He kissed me softly.

Below us, the water moved through the new surface channel, doing what water had always tried to do.

Finding somewhere safe to go.
